title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Microcytic hypochromic anemia, as the name suggests, is the type of anemia in which the circulating RBCs are smaller than the usual size of RBCs (microcytic) and have decreased red color pigment (hypochromic) from decreased hemoglobin production. The most common cause of this type of anemia is decreased iron reserves of the body, which may result from multiple different etiologies. These include reduced iron in the diet, poor absorption of iron from the gut in certain conditions, acute and chronic blood loss, and increased demand for iron in certain situations, like pregnancy or recovering from major trauma or surgery. Far less common causes include thalassemia and lead poisoning. Appropriately interpreting laboratory evaluations in the setting of clinical symptoms is key to diagnosing the etiology of anemia. This activity reviews the evaluation and management of microcytic hypochromic anemia and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in recognizing and managing this condition.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Introduction
content: Anemia is defined as the reduction in circulating red-cell mass below normal levels. Anemia is one of the most common chronic conditions worldwide and has significant morbidity. [1] Circulating red blood cells (RBCs) contain a protein known as hemoglobin, which has four polypeptide chains and one heme ring that contains iron in reduced form. [2] [3] Iron is the main component of hemoglobin and is the prime carrier of oxygen. Decreased iron reserves in the body affect the production of hemoglobin, which subsequently hinders the transport of oxygen to the organ systems of the body. Anemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and leads to tissue hypoxia. Usually, it is diagnosed by hematocrit (the ratio of packed RBCs to blood volume) and the hemoglobin concentration. The other major cause of microcytic hypochromic anemia is faulty production of alpha and beta globin chains, which are a result of different mutations in alpha and beta globin genes on chromosomes 16 and 11, respectively. The result of both low iron reserves or faulty hemoglobin chains is low MCV ( RBC volume <80 fL) and low hemoglobin content, which gives the condition its name, microcytic (small cell) hypochromic (decreased red coloring) anemia (low total hemoglobin). Less commonly, lead poisoning can interfere with hemoglobin synthesis and also cause this condition. [4] [5]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Etiology
content: Microcytic hypochromic anemia, as the name suggests, is the type of anemia in which the circulating RBCs are smaller than the usual size of RBCs (microcytic) and are pale with decreased red color (hypochromic). The most common cause is iron deficiency anemia (IDA), often due to chronic blood loss, poor intake, or malabsorption. This may be due to decreased iron in the diet, poor absorption of iron from the gut, acute and chronic blood loss, or increased demand for iron in certain situations, like pregnancy or recovering from major trauma or surgery. The other major cause of microcytosis with hypochromia is thalassemia syndromes, which are inherited disorders due to multiple different mutations in the (α or β) globin chains of hemoglobin, leading to reduced synthesis of hemoglobin. [1] [6]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Epidemiology
content: According to epidemiologic data from the World Health Organization (WHO), 24.8% to 32.9% of the human population is currently suffering from anemia, most commonly due to iron deficiency. Hypochromic, microcytic anemia is more common in premenopausal females because they lose blood with each menstrual cycle. Among the female population, almost 41% of all pregnant females suffer from anemia, while among nonpregnant premenopausal females, 30% of females have anemia. The male population is usually resistant to anemia due to circulating testosterone levels. However, globally, 12.7% of adult males are also afflicted with anemia. Pre-school-aged children are the second-highest group with anemia due to a lack of iron in their primary diet. Breast milk contains 0.3 mg/L iron, which is not sufficient for metabolism. Cow's milk contains double the amount of iron, but that iron has poor bioavailability and can interfere with the absorption of dietary iron from other sources. The WHO Global Nutrition Target 2025 on anemia aims to reduce anemia by 50% by 2025. [7]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: An adult human requires about 1 to 2 mg of iron per day to replace losses, and a typical Western diet provides 10 to 20 mg. Iron from animal sources is heme iron, with a bioavailability of approximately 10% to 20%. In contrast, non-heme iron has lower bioavailability (1%–5 %) due to inhibitors such as tannins, phytates, other food constituents, and different absorption mechanisms. [8] Gastric acid helps free iron from complexes, and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces ferric (Fe³ + ) to ferrous (Fe² + ) to prevent precipitation. Absorption occurs mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum via transporters (ie, HCP-1 and DMT1), and iron exits enterocytes through ferroportin into plasma, where transferrin carries it. Systemic regulation is mediated by hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin when iron is abundant or in inflammatory states. [9] [10] Iron is stored as ferritin (and hemosiderin) predominantly in liver parenchymal cells, macrophages in spleen, bone marrow, and skeletal muscle. Normal adult male body iron stores are more modest than often cited: total stored iron is 600 to 1,000 mg in males and 200 to 300 mg in females. [11]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Hypochromic microcytic anemia arises when iron supply or utilization is impaired such that hemoglobin synthesis is inadequate. In iron deficiency anemia, causes include low dietary iron, malabsorption (eg, celiac, chronic diarrhea, gastrectomy, inflammatory bowel disease), vitamin C deficiency, increased demands (eg, pregnancy, growth, surgery), or chronic/occult blood loss. The resulting RBCs are microcytic and hypochromic because of lower hemoglobin content.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: In thalassemias, a genetic defect in globin chain synthesis disrupts normal hemoglobin production. In β-thalassemia, deficient β-globin synthesis leads to excess free α-chains, which precipitate in erythroid precursors, triggering apoptosis and ineffective erythropoiesis. [12] Chronic anemia and hypoxia stimulate marrow hyperplasia and extramedullary hematopoiesis. Iron overload occurs both from increased absorption (due to suppressed hepcidin via erythroid signals like erythroferrone) and from repeated transfusions. [13] In α-thalassemia, reduced α-globin favors excess β- or γ-chains (depending on age), which similarly damage red cell precursors and shorten RBC lifespan. [14]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: The combination of defective globin synthesis, ineffective erythropoiesis, peripheral hemolysis, and iron overload distinguishes thalassemia pathophysiologically from pure iron deficiency, but mild thalassemia trait may present with mild microcytosis and normal iron parameters. [10] [11] [14] Please see StatPearls' companion references, " Alpha Thalassemia " and " Beta Thalassemia ."

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Less commonly, chronic lead poisoning can cause microcytic anemia, most commonly in children or those in developing countries. The most common exposures are environmental (ie, paint in older houses, water), occupational exposure, or consumption of lead-containing herbs. Signs of lead poisoning include weakness, abdominal pain, and neurologic symptoms. CLP can also cause microcytic anemia by interfering with the enzymes in hemoglobin production (ie, erythrocyte pyrimidine-specific, 5'-nucleotidase, erythrocyte nucleotidase). The result is microcytic hypochromic anemia, hemolytic anemia. Basophilic stippling in erythrocytes on Wright's staining from RNA clumping is pathognomonic for CLP. Please see StatPearls' companion reference "LeadToxicity" for further information. [15] [16] [17]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Histopathology
content: On peripheral smear, hypochromia is evident as an enlarged central zone of pallor (>1/3 of the RBC diameter) and a thin hemoglobinized rim. Microcytosis is reflected by a reduced MCV (<80 fL in adults with iron deficiency). In iron deficiency anemia (IDA), anisopoikilocytosis is common; pencil cells (elongated elliptocytes) and target cells may be present, with elevated RDW supporting heterogeneous cell sizes. Bone marrow in IDA shows reduced to absent stainable iron on Perls/Prussian blue staining of aspirate particles/macrophages; in severe deficiency, iron may be completely absent. Although bone marrow iron assessments remain the gold standard for documenting depleted iron stores, this is invasive and is now generally supplanted by ferritin-first algorithms. [18]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Histopathology
content: In thalassemias, peripheral smear also shows microcytosis and hypochromia, but typically with more uniform microcytosis (often normal RDW), numerous target cells, and sometimes basophilic stippling; overall RBC count is often normal/high relative to the degree of anemia. A-thalassemia (HbH disease) features HbH inclusion bodies (β4 tetramers) detectable on brilliant cresyl blue (supravital) staining. [19] β-thalassemia shows marrow erythroid hyperplasia with ineffective erythropoiesis—expansion of early erythroid precursors with apoptosis of late forms—driven by globin chain imbalance (excess unpaired α-chains), oxidative stress, and downstream hepcidin suppression; chronic cases develop extramedullary hematopoiesis and iron overload (from increased absorption ± transfusion). [20] Marrow iron stores in thalassemia are normal to increased (unless coexisting iron deficiency is present). [9] Ring sideroblasts are not a feature of thalassemia per se (they indicate sideroblastic processes/MDS), but Perls staining is routinely used in marrow evaluation to document iron distribution and exclude sideroblastic change when indicated. [21]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- History and Physical
content: The typical history indicates: Reduced dietary intake of iron Increased blood loss in menstrual flow Bleeding from the gut, particularly from gastric and duodenal ulcers Malignancy Major trauma after which iron stores become depleted. In some cases, pica may be present. This is a preference to eat non-nutritious substances like clay, ice, and flour.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- History and Physical
content: The patient may also report a sensation of food “sticking” in the chest due to esophageal webs, along with a swollen tongue (glossitis). This constellation of findings is consistent with Plummer–Vinson syndrome, a rare manifestation of iron deficiency.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- History and Physical
content: On physical exam, a patient may present with pallor evident on the hands as well as conjunctivitis, tachycardia, increased respiratory rate, exhaustion, and koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails). Severe anemia may also lead to the production of signs and symptoms of angina due to decreased delivery of oxygen to cardiac myocytes. [22]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Evaluation
content: The first diagnostic step after a complete clinical assessment is a complete blood count (CBC), which confirms anemia and provides critical red blood cell (RBC) indices. Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): Indicates RBC size; values <80 fL suggest microcytosis. Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC): Reflects hemoglobin content; reduced levels indicate hypochromia. Both parameters are decreased in microcytic hypochromic anemia, signifying impaired hemoglobin synthesis. [12] [23] The next step is a comprehensive iron panel.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Evaluation
content: Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC): Usually increased in iron deficiency anemia (IDA). Transferrin saturation: Markedly decreased in IDA (<15 %). Serum ferritin: Reflects body iron stores. Levels <15 ng/mL (some guidelines use <30 ng/mL) in the absence of infection strongly indicate IDA. Because ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, infections or chronic inflammation can elevate it; thus, a normal ferritin does not exclude IDA. As iron levels drop, transferrin production rises compensatorily. [24]

content: Peripheral smear typically shows microcytic RBCs with increased central pallor, a thin peripheral rim of hemoglobin, and pencil cells (elongated poikilocytes). These findings support hypochromic microcytic anemia due to iron deficiency.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Evaluation -- Evaluation for Thalassemias
content: When iron studies are normal or increased, thalassemia syndromes should be suspected. CBC patterns: Thalassemia often shows a normal or elevated RBC count despite anemia, very low MCV (<70 fL), and normal RDW (in contrast to IDA). Peripheral smear: Shows target cells, basophilic stippling, and uniform microcytosis. Hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC: In β-thalassemia trait, HbA2 is greater than 3.5 %, and sometimes HbF elevation is diagnostic. In α-thalassemia, electrophoresis may be normal; DNA analysis for α-globin gene deletions is required for confirmation. Ancillary markers: Reticulocyte hemoglobin content (CHr) or zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP) can differentiate iron deficiency from thalassemia. [25] [26] In cases where both coexist, iron studies and electrophoresis should be interpreted together.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Evaluation -- Evaluation for Lead
content: Evaluation is achieved by monitoring serum lead levels. Basophilic stippling on microscopy, along with symptoms of lead poisoning or microcytic hypochromic anemia, is pathognomonic for lead toxicity.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Treatment / Management
content: Once hypochromic microcytic anemia due to iron deficiency is confirmed, therapy aims to restore hemoglobin, replenish iron stores, and address the underlying cause.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Treatment / Management -- Oral Iron Therapy
content: The preferred treatment is oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental iron), once daily. Alternate-day dosing may enhance absorption and minimize hepcidin-induced suppression of iron uptake. [27] Gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, constipation, dark stools) are common; adherence can be improved by gradual dose titration or switching to ferrous gluconate or fumarate. Hemoglobin typically rises within 3 to 4 weeks, with normalization in 2 to 3 months if iron stores are replenished. After normalization, supplementation should be continued for at least 3 months to restore ferritin levels. Intravenous Iron Therapy IV formulations are indicated when oral iron is not tolerated or ineffective (malabsorption, chronic bleeding, inflammatory bowel disease).

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Treatment / Management
content: Common agents: ferric carboxymaltose, ferumoxytol, iron sucrose, or low-molecular-weight iron dextran. Total iron deficit can be estimated using the Ganzoni formula or simplified fixed dosing (eg, ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg × 2 doses 1 week apart). Parenteral iron replenishes stores faster and avoids compliance issues but requires monitoring for hypersensitivity and iron overload. [8]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Treatment / Management -- Thalassemia Syndromes
content: Thalassemias require a tailored approach based on transfusion dependence, iron overload, and ineffective erythropoiesis.

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Treatment / Management -- Transfusion support
content: Transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) requires regular packed RBC transfusions to maintain pretransfusion hemoglobin levels around 9 to 10.5 g/dL, suppressing marrow expansion and improving growth and organ function. [12]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Treatment / Management -- Iron chelation therapy
content: Chronic transfusion causes secondary iron overloadcan warrant chelation when serum ferritin is greater than 1,000 ng/mL or liver iron is greater than 3 mg/g dry weight. Chelating agents: Deferoxamine (parenteral) has been the gold standard for decades. Deferiprone (oral) is effective for cardiac iron. Deferasirox (oral) has a convenient once-daily dosing. Combination therapy (deferiprone + deferoxamine) offers superior cardiac protection.  [13]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Treatment / Management -- Emerging and adjunctive therapies
content: Luspatercept, an erythroid maturation agent, reduces transfusion burden by improving late-stage erythropoiesis by decreasing TGF-ß activity. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of anemia in patients with ß-thalassemia. [28] Gene-editing therapies (eg, CRISPR-Cas9 correction of β-globin) are under evaluation to normalize erythropoiesis and minimize iron loading. [29]

title: Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The diagnosis and management of hypochromic microcytic anemia is achieved with an interprofessional team that may include primary care providers, hospitalists, advanced practitioners, a gynecologist, hematologists, surgeons, and a gastroenterologist. The key is to determine the cause of the anemia. After the diagnosis of hypochromic microcytic anemia is established, oral iron replacement therapy can be commenced. Nausea and constipation are the side effects that limit the compliance of this therapy. Compliance can be increased by gradually increasing the dose of the treatment while monitoring the patient for side effects. The maximum tolerated dose is usually selected for the replacement of lost iron. The impact of this treatment usually appears after 3 weeks, while the full effects will be evident in 2 months. Close follow-up is required to ensure that the patient's hematocrit is improving. [30]
